input.question: An English speaker in 2016 can understand a 200 year old book from 1816 with relative ease. Would An English speaker from 1816 be able to understand Shakespeare's then 200 year old plays just as easily?
input.ground_truth: It's unlikely, but only because Shakespeare's locution wasn't customary in his time, but peculiar even then (source: any introduction to a recent edition of a Shakespeare work). If you were to switch this question to some other author of the same period, though, I'm not sure. Edit: I also want to challenge the claim that we can understand texts from 1816 with relative ease. Academics can, but can most English speakers really deal with the crazy punctuation, tortuously long sentences, and GRE-level vocabulary?

Question: An English speaker in 2016 can understand a 200 year old book from 1816 with relative ease. Would An English speaker from 1816 be able to understand Shakespeare's then 200 year old plays just as easily?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a toy that was made 200 years ago. If you get that toy now in 2016, you can still play with it because toys don’t change much. But language is like a game with rules, and the rules can change over time.

Let’s say you (in 2016) get a book from 1816. The words might look a little old, but you can still read and understand them because the English language hasn’t changed too much in 200 years.

But if someone from 1816 tried to read a play written by Shakespeare, who wrote about 200 years before them (so, around 1600), it would be much harder! The words and the way people talked back then were very different. It’s like if you got a toy from 400 years ago—it might not even look like a toy anymore!

So, the person in 1816 would find Shakespeare’s plays much harder to understand than you would find a book from 1816.
